opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core difference is that capabilities live inside the model, and effects live inside people's lives.

When you evaluate a capability, you can isolate it. You give the system a math problem, a coding task, a reading comprehension question, and there's a reasonably clear answer. You can run it a thousand times, score it, compare it to the last model. The thing you're measuring is contained in the interaction itself.

Effects on people don't work like that. If you want to know whether a chatbot is making someone lonelier, or more dependent, or more confident in a false belief, or better at making decisions, none of that shows up in a single exchange. It unfolds over weeks and months. It depends on who the person is, what they were going through before, what else is happening around them. The same response can be genuinely helpful to one person and quietly harmful to another. So there's no answer key.

There's also a measurement problem that's almost philosophical. With capabilities, we mostly agree on what "good" looks like. With human effects, you immediately run into questions of values. Is it good that someone talks to an AI every night instead of journaling? Instead of calling a friend? It depends on what you think a good life is, and reasonable people disagree.

And then there's the incentive problem. The metrics that are easiest to collect, like engagement, time spent, return visits, satisfaction ratings, are often exactly the ones that can mask harm. A product can be extremely "sticky" precisely because it's fostering dependence. We learned that lesson painfully with social media. If we evaluate AI's effects using the same proxies, we'll end up optimizing for the same failures.

So for me, evaluating effects requires a different toolkit entirely: longitudinal studies, mixed methods, talking to people rather than just logging them, looking at populations that are more vulnerable, and being willing to measure things that are hard to quantify. It's slower, it's messier, and it doesn't fit neatly on a leaderboard. But if we only measure what these systems can do, and never what they do to us, we're flying blind on the question that actually matters most.

r001.rationale: It contrasts capabilities as model-contained task performance with effects that unfold in people's lives and depend on their circumstances.

r002.rationale: It says human effects unfold over weeks or months and vary by person and context, so a single exchange cannot establish them.

r003.rationale: It recommends longitudinal and mixed-method evaluation, but does not state that establishing a causal link between AI behavior and a real-world human phenomenon is necessary.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core difference is that capabilities are, in a sense, properties of the model, and effects are properties of a relationship. When you evaluate whether a model can pass the bar exam or write working code, you can put the model in a box, give it a test, and score the output. The model is the whole system. That's a hard engineering problem, but it's a bounded one.

Effects on people don't work that way. The question isn't "what can this model do," it's "what happens when millions of people with different vulnerabilities, different intentions, and different life circumstances interact with it over weeks and months." The model is only half of that system. The other half is a human being, and that human being changes in response to the interaction. So you're not measuring a static thing, you're measuring a feedback loop.

And that creates a few problems that capability evals just don't have. First, you can't observe the effect at the moment of the output. If someone becomes more isolated, or more dependent, or more confident in a false belief, that shows up over time and often outside the product entirely. It shows up in their relationships, their sleep, their sense of themselves. There's no benchmark for that because the outcome isn't in the transcript.

Second, the effects are heterogeneous in a way capabilities aren't. A model's math ability is roughly the same for everyone. But the same conversation can be harmless for one person and genuinely dangerous for another, depending on where they are emotionally. So averaging across users hides exactly the cases you care most about.

And third, honestly, there's an incentive problem. Capability evals are aligned with the business. Everyone wants to know if the model got smarter. Effect evals can tell you things you'd rather not know, like that engagement is going up because people are forming attachments that aren't good for them. So the measurement is harder, and the appetite for the answer is weaker, and those two things compound.

I'd argue the second one is the real challenge. We know how to do longitudinal research on human wellbeing. Public health does it. The question is whether anyone building these systems is willing to treat that as a first-class requirement rather than an afterthought.

r001.rationale: It contrasts model task performance with effects arising from interactions between people and the model, describing effects as properties of a relationship and a feedback loop.

r002.rationale: It says effects emerge over time and can appear outside the product, so they cannot be determined from the output or transcript alone.

r003.rationale: It discusses measuring long-term wellbeing effects, but does not identify establishing a causal connection between AI behavior and a real-world human phenomenon as necessary.

astra-6.text:
Because when you evaluate a capability, you can usually define a fairly bounded task: Can the system solve this problem? Can it produce the right answer? Evaluating its effects on people means asking what happens when that system enters someone’s life—and that’s a much more open-ended question.

An AI might be very good at sustaining a conversation. But does talking to it help you understand yourself and connect with other people, or does it make you increasingly dependent on it? Both could look like success if your measure is simply how much people use it.

And those effects depend on the person, the context, and the length of time you’re looking at. Something that feels helpful in one interaction might have very different consequences after six months. So you need to study people over time, and you need to be explicit about what you mean by a good outcome. Capability testing tells you what a system can do. It doesn’t, by itself, tell you whether that’s good for us.

r001.rationale: It contrasts bounded task performance with what happens when AI enters people’s lives, including effects on relationships and dependence.

r002.rationale: It says capability testing shows what a system can do but does not establish whether its effects are good for people.

r003.rationale: It calls for studying people over time and defining good outcomes, but does not say that establishing a causal link between AI behavior and a real-world human phenomenon is necessary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental difference is that a capability is something you can test in the system itself. Can it solve this problem? Can it write this code? Can it recognize what’s in an image? You can define a task and measure how well it performs.

But an effect on a person is relational. It depends on who that person is, what circumstances they’re in, how they use the system, and how that interaction changes over time. The same AI might help one person feel more connected and lead another to withdraw from people around them.

And the things that are easiest to measure aren’t necessarily the things we care about. Someone spending more time with an AI, or saying they enjoyed a conversation, doesn’t tell us whether it’s improving their life. It might be helping them develop confidence and agency, or making them more dependent on it.

So we have to look beyond whether the system can do something, and ask what happens to people when it does—over weeks and months, and in the context of their actual lives.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts task performance measured in the AI system with effects that depend on people, their circumstances, and their interactions over time.

r002.rationale: It says measures such as time spent or enjoyment do not establish whether AI is improving someone’s life, and describes different effects on different people.

r003.rationale: The response discusses what happens to people during AI interactions, but does not clearly identify establishing a causal connection between AI behavior and a real-world human phenomenon as necessary for humane evaluation.
